# Introduction

This application estimates the **total number of species expected to exist** in a
taxonomic group ($S_T$) from a time series of species descriptions, using a
Bayesian hierarchical model. It generalizes the framework applied to Brazilian
Dactylogyridae (parasitic flatworms) and their freshwater Actinopterygii (bony
fish) hosts in Boeger et al. (submitted, *Zoologia*, manuscript
ZOOL-2026-0012.R1), which in turn adapts the species-discovery models of Pimm
et al. (2010) and Joppa et al. (2011).

**The app is not restricted to any particular taxon.** You supply your own
species-description records (any parasitic or free-living group), and the app
fits the model to *your* data with *your* priors.

Two modes are supported:

- **Parasitic** — includes an optional host-availability covariate, for
  groups with a definable, boundable host pool (e.g., a parasite family and
  its host order).
- **Free-living** — no host covariate; appropriate for any taxon without a
  meaningful host-limitation term (e.g., free-living fish, insects, plants).

No dataset, credential, or analysis result is stored by the application beyond
your browser session. See §7 ("Data Handling & Privacy") for details.

# Scientific Background & Method

## The discovery process

The number of *new* species described in time interval $i$, $S_i$, is modeled
as a random draw from a Poisson process whose rate depends on (a) how many
species remain to be discovered, (b) how much taxonomic effort was applied,
and, for parasitic taxa, (c) how many host species remain available to be
surveyed:

$$
\log \lambda_i \;=\; \underbrace{(\log L_0 + \beta \cdot Y_i)}_{\text{taxonomic efficiency at time } Y_i}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log(S_T - \text{cumS}_i)}_{\text{species remaining}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log(H_t - \text{cumH}_i)}_{\text{hosts remaining (parasitic mode only)}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log(1 + T_i)}_{\text{effort}}
$$

$$
S_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $S_T$ | **Total number of species expected to exist** in the group — the key quantity of interest. |
| $L_0$ | Baseline taxonomic discovery efficiency (species described per unit of remaining diversity, per taxonomist, at the reference year). Fit on the log scale as $\log L_0$. |
| $\beta$ | Trend in discovery efficiency over time. Positive = taxonomists are getting relatively more efficient at finding remaining species over time; negative = the opposite (e.g., the "easy" species were found first). |
| $Y_i$ | Centered end-year of interval $i$ (years minus the mean year, so the intercept $L_0$ refers to the middle of your time series, not year zero). |
| $\text{cumS}_i$ | Cumulative species described **before** interval $i$ began. |
| $T_i$ | Number of unique taxonomists (authors) active in interval $i$ — a proxy for research effort. |
| $H_t$ | Total known/expected host-species pool (parasitic mode only) — a fixed number you supply, not fitted. |
| $\text{cumH}_i$ | Cumulative unique host species recorded **before** interval $i$ (parasitic mode only; computed automatically from your `animalHostNames` column). |

Intuitively: as more species are described ($\text{cumS}_i$ grows toward
$S_T$), the pool of undescribed species shrinks, and the expected discovery
rate declines — unless rising effort ($T_i$) or efficiency ($L_0, \beta$)
compensates. Fitting this model to your observed $(S_i, T_i)$ time series lets
the Bayesian posterior on $S_T$ tell you, with uncertainty, how many species
are likely to exist in total — including the ones not yet described.

## Why Bayesian, and why priors matter

$S_T$ is not identified by the data alone in any strict sense — the model
extrapolates a decelerating discovery curve toward an asymptote it has not
yet observed. The **prior on $S_T$** (a Gamma distribution, parameterized by
shape `alpha` and rate `beta`, with prior mean $= \alpha/\beta$) is therefore
not a formality: it encodes your independent, external belief about the
plausible order of magnitude of total diversity (e.g., from comparable taxa,
expert judgement, or published estimates for sister groups). **The app does
not supply a default $S_T$ prior — you must set one explicitly**, because a
sensible default does not exist across arbitrary taxa. See §4.2 for practical
guidance on choosing `alpha`/`beta`.

The $\log L_0$ and $\beta$ priors are weaker (default: Normal(0, 2) and
Normal(0, 0.1) respectively) and rarely need adjustment unless you have strong
prior knowledge about the trend in discovery efficiency.

## Structural variants: host vs. no-host

- **Host structure** (parasitic mode only) adds the $\log(H_t - \text{cumH}_i)$
  term, reflecting the hypothesis that parasite discovery is partly
  contingent on finding new host species to examine. You supply $H_t$ (a
  single fixed number: your best estimate of the total host-species pool)
  and the app computes $\text{cumH}_i$ automatically from the
  `animalHostNames` column.
- **No-host structure** omits that term. It is the only option in free-living
  mode, and is also available in parasitic mode so you can directly compare
  whether the host covariate improves the model for your data (as done in
  the source manuscript, where host models were found to outperform no-host
  models).

## Model fitting

Models are fit with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan, via `rstan`), sampling
$S_T$, $\log L_0$, and $\beta$ from their joint posterior. You control the
number of iterations, warmup, and chains (§4.4); more iterations give more
stable estimates at the cost of runtime.

**Convergence diagnostics** (`Rhat`, `n_eff`) are reported alongside every
parameter estimate. As a rule of thumb, `Rhat` should be $\le 1.01$ and
`n_eff` should be in the hundreds or more; if not, increase iterations/warmup
or reconsider the priors.

## Comparing models: the sensitivity battery

A single run fits **one** prior specification with **one or two** structures.
The **sensitivity battery** (§4.3) instead lets you define several prior
scenarios and fits every scenario against every selected structure, then
ranks all resulting models by:

- **LOO-ELPD** (Leave-One-Out Expected Log Predictive Density, via the `loo`
  package): a fully Bayesian estimate of each model's out-of-sample
  generalization. Higher (less negative) is better.
- **CRPS** (Continuous Ranked Probability Score) and **MAE** (Mean Absolute
  Error) of the posterior-predictive distribution against your observed
  $S_i$ time series (via `scoringRules`). Lower is better for both.

Reporting results across multiple priors, rather than a single arbitrarily
chosen one, is standard practice for demonstrating that your conclusions are
not an artifact of one prior choice — this is exactly the analysis performed
in the source manuscript across six prior scenarios.

# Data Requirements

Upload an `.xlsx` or `.csv` file. Column names must match **exactly** (case
sensitive). Any other columns in your file are ignored.

## Always required

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `scientificName` | text | The species' scientific name. Used to count distinct species per year. |
| `namePublishedInYear` | number | The year the species was formally described/published. |
| `scientificNameAuthorship` | text | The describing author(s), e.g. `"Smith, J. & Jones, A."`. Used only to count unique active taxonomists per year (the effort proxy $T_i$). Names are split on commas, semicolons, ampersands, and the standalone words "and"/"e"/"y" (English/Portuguese/Spanish conjunctions). |

## Required in Parasitic mode only

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `animalHostNames` | text | Semicolon-separated list of host species names for that record, e.g. `"Hostus one; Hostus two"`. Used to compute the cumulative unique-host time series ($\text{cumH}_i$). |

## Data preparation tips

- One row per species record (not per specimen or per locality).
- Filter your source data to the taxon and time window you want modeled
  *before* uploading — the app does not filter by higher taxonomy; it treats
  every row in the uploaded file as belonging to the target group.
- Rows with a missing/non-numeric year, missing species name, or (in
  parasitic mode) missing host names are dropped automatically, with the
  cleaned row count shown after upload.
- If your data spans a very long time range with few early records, consider
  setting a later **start year** (§4.1) to exclude a sparse, uninformative
  tail that can destabilize the fit.

# Using the App — Step by Step

## Login

Enter the shared password on the landing page. There are no individual user
accounts; anyone with the password has full access.

## Tab 1 — Data & Setup

1. Choose **Group type**: Parasitic or Free-living. This determines which
   data columns are required and which model structures are available later.
2. Enter a **Taxon name** — free text, used only to label plots and the
   downloadable report.
3. **Upload** your `.xlsx`/`.csv` file. A validation banner confirms the row
   count or reports the first missing/invalid column.
4. Set the **interval width** (in years) that species counts are aggregated
   into (e.g., 3 or 5 years — matching the interval width used in the
   Dactylogyridae/Actinopterygii analyses). Smaller intervals give more data
   points but noisier per-interval counts; larger intervals smooth noise but
   reduce the number of time points available to fit the trend.
5. Optionally set a **start year** / **end year** to restrict the modeled
   window (defaults to the full range present in your data).
6. In parasitic mode, enter **$H_t$** — your best estimate of the total host
   species pool, as a plain number (not fitted).
7. Review the **aggregated interval table** at the bottom of the page — this
   is the exact $S_i$/$T_i$/$\text{cumS}_i$(/$\text{cumH}_i$) time series that
   will be passed to the model. Check it for implausible jumps or gaps before
   proceeding.

## Tab 2 — Priors & Run

1. **Structures to fit**: in parasitic mode, choose "with host covariate",
   "without", or both (both is recommended, to let the LOO/CRPS comparison
   tell you which fits your data better); free-living mode offers only the
   no-host structure.
2. **Single run vs. battery**: leave "Run full sensitivity battery" unchecked
   for a fast, single-prior run (recommended for initial exploration).
   Check it to instead define and compare several prior scenarios (§4.3).
3. **Single-run priors**: enter the Gamma($\alpha$, $\beta$) prior for $S_T$
   (no default — see §2.2 and the guidance box below), and optionally adjust
   the $\log L_0$ and $\beta$ priors (weak defaults provided).

   > **Choosing $\alpha$/$\beta$ for the $S_T$ prior:** the Gamma
   > distribution's mean is $\alpha/\beta$. A simple approach: pick a rough
   > expected total species count $m$ from external knowledge (a comparable
   > taxon, an expert guess, a published order-of-magnitude estimate), pick a
   > shape $\alpha$ reflecting your confidence (larger $\alpha$ = tighter,
   > more confident prior; $\alpha \approx 20$–100 is a reasonably informative
   > but not overly rigid choice), then set $\beta = \alpha / m$. The prior's
   > lower bound is automatically constrained to exceed your observed
   > cumulative species count, so $S_T$ can never be estimated below what
   > you've already described.

4. **Battery scenarios**: fill in the scenario form (name + all four prior
   parameters) and click "Add scenario"; repeat for each scenario you want
   compared. "Clear all scenarios" resets the list.
5. **MCMC settings**: default iterations (4000) and warmup (2000) with 4
   chains are adequate for exploration; check "Full precision" (20000/10000)
   for a final, publication-quality run once you're satisfied with your setup
   — this is substantially slower.
6. Click **Run analysis**. Only one analysis runs at a time across *all*
   users of the app (a shared compute worker) — if others are running jobs,
   yours will start once theirs finishes. The status box shows elapsed time
   while waiting/running.

## Tab 3 — Results

For a **single run**, each fitted structure ("with"/"without host
covariate") shows:

- **Parameter table**: mean, 95% credible interval, and convergence
  diagnostics (`Rhat`, `n_eff`) for $S_T$, $\log L_0$, $L_0$, and $\beta$.
- **Posterior histogram** and **trace plot** for $S_T$ — the trace plot
  should look like a "hairy caterpillar" with no trend or stuck chains; if
  it doesn't, increase iterations/warmup.
- **Simulated vs. observed plot** (posterior predictive check): blue lines
  are simulated discovery-rate trajectories drawn from the fitted model; the
  red line is your actual observed data. The red line should sit
  comfortably within the cloud of blue lines if the model fits well.
- **Percent-described plot**: the posterior distribution of
  (observed total) / $S_T$, i.e., what fraction of the estimated true
  diversity has been described so far.
- **Extrapolation plot**: your observed cumulative-discovery curve, plus a
  forward projection (with 95% credible band) assuming future taxonomic
  effort continues at the recent average level.

For a **battery run**: a ranked comparison table (every scenario × structure,
with $S_T$ estimates, LOO-ELPD, CRPS, MAE), plus comparison plots. The
best-supported model by LOO-ELPD is called out explicitly.

## Tab 4 — Download Report

Generates a single self-contained HTML file bundling every figure, the
parameter table(s), the methods description, and a data-handling notice —
built fresh from your current results, never stored server-side. Useful for
supplementary material, sharing with collaborators, or your own records.

## About

A short in-app summary of scope and data handling; this manual is the
complete reference.

# Interpreting the Diagnostic Plots (Reference)

| Plot | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Posterior histogram ($S_T$) | A unimodal, reasonably concentrated distribution. A histogram that looks identical to your prior means the data contributed little information — consider a longer/less sparse time series or a more informative prior. |
| Trace plot | Overlapping, stationary "hairy caterpillar" traces across chains, no drift or sudden jumps. |
| Simulated vs. observed | Red observed line inside the blue simulation envelope, most of the time. Persistent misses indicate model misspecification (e.g., missing the host term, or an interval width that's too coarse/fine). |
| Percent-described | Sanity-check this against domain knowledge — an implausibly low or high percentage may indicate a prior that's too far from the data (revisit $\alpha$/$\beta$). |
| Extrapolation | The credible band should widen (not narrow) further into the future — a band that stays razor-thin suggests overconfidence, usually from an overly tight $S_T$ prior. |
| Effort vs. discovery scatter | A rough positive relationship supports the model's core assumption that more taxonomists means more species found. A flat or negative relationship is a warning sign worth investigating before trusting $S_T$. |
| LOO-ELPD / CRPS / MAE (battery) | Prefer models that rank well on **both** ELPD and CRPS; large disagreement between the two metrics for a given model is itself informative (see §2.5 and the source manuscript's discussion of this exact situation). |

# Data Handling & Privacy

- **Nothing is stored.** Your uploaded file, the fitted model object, and
  every generated figure exist only in your browser session's server-side
  scratch space, in memory/temp-disk for the lifetime of that session.
- **No database.** The application does not use any persistent database —
  not for your data, not for results, not even temporarily.
- **Session end = deletion.** When your browser tab closes or the session
  times out, all session data is deleted automatically.
- **You must download before leaving.** The report (Tab 4) is the only way
  to keep a copy of your results; nothing is retrievable after the session
  ends.
- **Authentication** uses a single shared password (not stored in plaintext
  anywhere in the deployed application — only its SHA-256 hash is kept as a
  server secret) and a per-session flag; there are no individual accounts,
  audit logs, or password-reset flows.

# Troubleshooting / FAQ

**"Missing required column(s)" on upload.**
Column names must match exactly, including case (`scientificName`, not
`ScientificName` or `Scientific_Name`). Check §3 for the exact required set
per mode.

**"Fewer than 3 usable time intervals after aggregation."**
Your data, after filtering and interval aggregation, doesn't span enough
distinct time buckets to fit a trend. Widen your start/end year range, or
reduce the interval width.

**Run seems stuck on "Running…".**
Only one analysis runs at a time across all users — you may be queued behind
another user's job, especially a full-precision or battery run. There is no
separate progress bar for queue position; the elapsed-time counter includes
any wait.

**High `Rhat` / low `n_eff` warnings.**
Increase iterations and warmup (or enable "Full precision"), and/or
double-check that your $S_T$ prior isn't so tight that it conflicts sharply
with the data (this can create hard-to-sample posterior geometry).

**"Enter a valid $S_T$ Gamma prior" error on Run.**
The app deliberately has no default $S_T$ prior (§2.2) — `alpha` and `beta`
must both be entered and positive before a single run can start.

**Host structure unavailable in my mode.**
The host covariate is only available in Parasitic mode with an `Ht` value
supplied; Free-living mode always uses the no-host structure only.

# Glossary

- **$S_T$** — total number of species estimated to exist in the group (the
  primary output of the model).
- **Interval** — a fixed-width block of consecutive years (e.g., a 5-year
  bin) used to aggregate species counts for model fitting.
- **Effort ($T_i$)** — number of unique describing taxonomists active in an
  interval, used as a proxy for research intensity.
- **Credible interval (CrI)** — the Bayesian analogue of a confidence
  interval; a 95% CrI means the posterior probability that the true value
  lies in that range is 95%, given the model and data.
- **LOO-ELPD** — Leave-One-Out Expected Log Predictive Density; a Bayesian
  model-comparison metric estimating out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
- **CRPS / MAE** — Continuous Ranked Probability Score / Mean Absolute Error;
  metrics comparing a model's simulated predictions to observed data.
- **Rhat, n_eff** — MCMC convergence diagnostics; see §2.4.
